scenes.visual: Title card: What Limits a Population? Show a crab population surrounded by food, shelter, predators and cold water. No spoken narration.

scenes.tts: The number of blue crabs in the Chesapeake Bay can change by more than one hundred million from one winter to the next. But no population can keep growing forever. Food and hiding places are limited. Predators, disease, temperature and salinity affect survival too. Together, resources and challenges set the largest population an environment can support over time. That is its carrying capacity.

scenes.visual: Open on the Bay and a crab population with the label “Winter population estimates can change by more than 100 million.” Immediately reveal limited food and hiding places, then predators, disease, temperature and salinity. Group these as resources and challenges. Define carrying capacity on screen as the largest population the environment can support over time. Do not present annual counts as carrying capacity.

scenes.tts: A population is one species in one place at one time. A limiting factor keeps it from growing larger. Biotic factors are living parts of the environment, like predators and disease. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, like temperature and salinity, the salt level. Crowding makes competition and disease worse.
scenes.visual: Keep the crab population box. Label it “One species, one place, one time.” Show green biotic arrows for predators and disease and orange abiotic arrows for temperature and salinity. Add limited food and shelter; increase competition and disease as the crab tokens crowd together.

scenes.tts: Suppose ten bacteria land in a dish of fresh food. Each one splits in two every thirty minutes. Now there are twenty, then forty, eighty, one hundred sixty, and three hundred twenty. This is exponential growth. It makes a J shape while resources are plentiful.
scenes.caption: Suppose 10 bacteria land in a dish of fresh food. Each one splits in two every 30 minutes. Now there are 20, then 40, 80, 160, and 320. This is exponential growth. It makes a J shape while resources are plentiful.
scenes.visual: Retain the bacteria example and bars for 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and 320. Join the tops with a J-shaped curve. Label this a plentiful-resources example, with time and population-size axes.
scenes.narration: Suppose 10 bacteria land in a dish of fresh food. Each one splits in two every 30 minutes. Now there are 20, then 40, 80, 160, and 320. This is exponential growth. It makes a J shape while resources are plentiful.

scenes.tts: Then limits set in. Food runs short. In the simplest model, growth slows into an S shape and levels off near carrying capacity. If few individuals move in or out, births and deaths are about equal there. Small ups and downs around that level are called dynamic equilibrium.
scenes.visual: On axes labelled “Model, made-up units,” show food becoming limited and the growth curve bending into an S. Keep a dashed carrying-capacity line. At the plateau, show balanced births and deaths, with little movement in or out, and small population wobbles. Label dynamic equilibrium. Present the curve as a model.

scenes.tts: Carrying capacity can change when food, space or shelter change and stay changed. More hiding places can raise it. Losing marsh grass can lower it. A single hard freeze is different. If resources stay the same, it pushes the population below carrying capacity, and the population can grow back. Crabbing also removes individuals. Fewer crabs does not by itself mean a lower carrying capacity.
scenes.visual: Use separate model panels. In the first, lasting gains in shelter raise the dashed capacity line; loss of marsh lowers it. In the second, a single freeze drops the population curve while resources and the capacity line stay unchanged, followed by recovery. Show crabbing removing crab tokens without automatically lowering the capacity line. Label population size and carrying capacity separately.

Fewer crabs does not by itself mean a lower carrying capacity.

scenes.tts: What does the winter survey show? In the last two survey winters, the total rose mostly because there were more young crabs. Adult females fell. These are population estimates. The survey does not measure carrying capacity or tell us which factor caused the change. We need temperature, habitat and predator data to test that. The central rule is that environmental limits constrain population growth.
scenes.visual: Show a dredge sampling crabs, then compare the lesson’s 2024–2025 and 2025–2026 survey winters. Label the comparison as estimates: total up, juveniles up, adult females down. Use arrows without invented counts. State “Survey estimates population size; it does not measure carrying capacity or identify the cause.” Show temperature, habitat and predator data as evidence needed to test causes. Finish with “Environmental limits constrain population growth.”
